claim: The oxaloacetate decarboxylase sodium pump (OAD) utilizes the free energy derived from oxaloacetate decarboxylation for sodium transport across the cell membrane.
source: The oxaloacetate decarboxylase sodium pump (OAD) is a unique primary-active transporter that utilizes the free energy derived from oxaloacetate decarboxylation for sodium transport across the cell membrane.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and introduction, and is supported by the functional studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: OAD is composed of 3 subunits: α, β, and γ.
source: It is composed of 3 subunits: the α subunit catalyzes carboxyl-transfer from oxaloacetate to biotin, the membrane integrated β subunit catalyzes the subsequent carboxyl-biotin decarboxylation and the coupled sodium transport, the γ subunit interacts with the α and β subunits and stabilizes the OAD complex.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and confirmed by the structural and biochemical data presented.

claim: The α subunit catalyzes carboxyl-transfer from oxaloacetate to biotin.
source: It is composed of 3 subunits: the α subunit catalyzes carboxyl-transfer from oxaloacetate to biotin, the membrane integrated β subunit catalyzes the subsequent carboxyl-biotin decarboxylation and the coupled sodium transport, the γ subunit interacts with the α and β subunits and stabilizes the OAD complex.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is consistent with established knowledge about OAD function.

claim: The β subunit catalyzes carboxyl-biotin decarboxylation and the coupled sodium transport.
source: It is composed of 3 subunits: the α subunit catalyzes carboxyl-transfer from oxaloacetate to biotin, the membrane integrated β subunit catalyzes the subsequent carboxyl-biotin decarboxylation and the coupled sodium transport, the γ subunit interacts with the α and β subunits and stabilizes the OAD complex.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the functional assays showing that β subunit mutations affect sodium binding and oxaloacetate decarboxylation.

claim: The γ subunit interacts with the α and β subunits and stabilizes the OAD complex.
source: It is composed of 3 subunits: the α subunit catalyzes carboxyl-transfer from oxaloacetate to biotin, the membrane integrated β subunit catalyzes the subsequent carboxyl-biotin decarboxylation and the coupled sodium transport, the γ subunit interacts with the α and β subunits and stabilizes the OAD complex.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the structural data showing extensive interactions between β and γ subunits, and by the γΔCT experiments.

claim: The β and γ subunits form a β3γ3 hetero-hexamer.
source: The structure revealed that the β and γ subunits form a β3γ3 hetero-hexamer with extensive interactions between the subunits and shed light on the OAD holo-enzyme assembly.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the cryo-EM structure and dynamic light scattering data.

claim: The β3γ3 hetero-hexamer has extensive interactions between the subunits.
source: The structure revealed that the β and γ subunits form a β3γ3 hetero-hexamer with extensive interactions between the subunits and shed light on the OAD holo-enzyme assembly.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by the structural analysis showing buried surface areas of 2700 Å2 between β subunits and 3100 Å2 between β and γ subunits.

claim: OAD is the first identified sodium pump responsible for maintaining the sodium gradient in microorganisms.
source: The oxaloacetate decarboxylase sodium pump (OAD) is the first identified sodium pump responsible for maintaining the sodium gradient in microorganisms (Dimroth, 1980).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Dimroth, 1980.

claim: OAD is found in many bacteria and archaea including the human pathogens Klebsiella aerogenes, Klebsiella pneumonia, Salmonella typhimurium and Legionella pneumophila.
source: It is found in many bacteria and archaea including the human pathogens Klebsiella aerogenes (Dimroth, 1980), Klebsiella pneumonia (Schwarz et al., 1988), Salmonella typhimurium (Wifling and Dimroth, 1989) and Legionella pneumophila (Jain et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to multiple studies.

claim: OAD plays a critical role in the anaerobic citrate fermentation pathway.
source: It plays a critical role in the anaerobic citrate fermentation pathway (Dimroth et al., 2001), and has been shown to be important for the pathogenicity of certain pathogens (Hwang et al., 1992; Jain et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Dimroth et al., 2001.

claim: OAD has been shown to be important for the pathogenicity of certain pathogens.
source: It plays a critical role in the anaerobic citrate fermentation pathway (Dimroth et al., 2001), and has been shown to be important for the pathogenicity of certain pathogens (Hwang et al., 1992; Jain et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Hwang et al., 1992 and Jain et al., 1996.

claim: Biotin serves as the carrier for the carboxyl group in the OAD reaction and is covalently linked to the biotin-carboxyl carrier protein (BCCP) domain in the α subunit C terminus.
source: Biotin serves as the carrier for the carboxyl group in its reaction and is covalently linked to the biotin-carboxyl carrier protein (BCCP) domain in the α subunit C terminus.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is consistent with established knowledge about biotin-dependent enzymes.

claim: OAD belongs to the decarboxylase sodium pump family.
source: OAD belongs to the decarboxylase sodium pump family (Buckel, 2001; Dimroth et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Buckel, 2001 and Dimroth et al., 2001.

claim: Members of the decarboxylase sodium pump family include methylmalonyl-CoA decarboxylases (MCD), glutaconyl-CoA decarboxylase (GCD) and malonate decarboxylase (MAD).
source: Members in this family also include methylmalonyl-CoA decarboxylases (MCD), glutaconyl-CoA decarboxylase (GCD) and malonate decarboxylase (MAD).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is consistent with established classification of these enzymes.

claim: Decarboxylase sodium pumps constitute a unique family of primary-active transporters.
source: They utilize the free energy derived from decarboxylating the relevant substrates to drive sodium transport across the cell membrane, and constitute a unique family of primary-active transporters (Saier et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Saier et al., 2016.

claim: The β subunits of MCD and GCD are highly homologous to the OAD β subunit.
source: Their β subunits are highly homologous to the OAD β subunit (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of the StOAD βγ sub-complex was determined to an overall resolution of 3.88 Å.
source: We carried out cryo-EM experiments and determined its structure (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a–d) to an overall resolution of 3.88 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 3e).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the FSC curve in Figure 1—figure supplement 3e.

claim: Resolution of the core regions of the StOAD βγ sub-complex reaches 3.6 Å.
source: Resolution of the core regions reaches 3.6 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 3f).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the local resolution map in Figure 1—figure supplement 3f.

claim: Residues 13–432 in the β subunit were placed in the cryo-EM structure.
source: The excellent density (Figure 1—figure supplement 4a–e) allowed us to place all the non-hydrogen atoms for residues 13–432 in the β subunit.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the density maps shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Residues 2–43 in the γ subunit were assigned based on secondary structure prediction and density features.
source: Since most residues in the β subunit were accounted for, residues 2–43 in the γ subunit were assigned to this helix based on secondary structure prediction and density features.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on inference from the density and secondary structure predictions.

claim: 100 mM of sodium chloride was included in the protein buffer during structure determination.
source: Although 100 mM of sodium chloride was included in the protein buffer, no obvious densities for sodium ions were observed, probably due to the moderate resolution.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the experimental conditions.

claim: No obvious densities for sodium ions were observed in the cryo-EM structure, probably due to the moderate resolution.
source: Although 100 mM of sodium chloride was included in the protein buffer, no obvious densities for sodium ions were observed, probably due to the moderate resolution.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and represents an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: The crystal structure of the βγ sub-complex was determined using the cryo-EM structure as the search model.
source: Using the cryo-EM structure as the search model, we determined the crystal structure of the βγ sub-complex by molecular replacement (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the crystallographic methods.

claim: No major conformational differences were found between the cryo-EM and the crystal structures of the βγ sub-complex.
source: No major conformational differences were found between the cryo-EM and the crystal structures.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on comparison of the two structures.

claim: One side of the β subunit trimer is predominantly positively charged, the opposite side is negatively charged.
source: One side of the β subunit trimer is predominantly positively charged, the opposite side is negatively charged (Figure 1c–d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in the electrostatic surface representations in Figure 1c-d.

claim: The 'positive inside rule' indicates that the positively charged side of the β subunit trimer is located in the cytoplasm.
source: The 'positive inside rule' (von Heijne, 1992) indicates that the positively charged side is located in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the established 'positive inside rule' for membrane protein topology.

claim: The positively charged side of the β subunit trimer is concentrated with conserved residues.
source: This side is also concentrated with conserved residues (Figure 1—figure supplement 5a–d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in the conservation mapping in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The structure revealed no solvent accessible channels connecting the cytoplasm and the periplasm in the β subunit.
source: The structure revealed no solvent accessible channels connecting the cytoplasm and the periplasm.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of the structure.

claim: The γ subunit C-terminal tail is located in the cytoplasm and could mediate interactions with the α subunit.
source: The structure indicates that the γ subunit C-terminal tail is located in the cytoplasm and could mediate interactions with the α subunit (Figure 1a–b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the structural data and inference about function.

claim: The isolated γ subunit C-terminal tail interacts with the α subunit.
source: This is in line with previous reports that the isolated γ subunit C-terminal tail interacts with the α subunit (Balsera et al., 2011; Dahinden et al., 2005), and the α subunit fails to interact with γ subunit variants with mutations or deletions in this region (Schmid et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to previous studies.

claim: The α subunit fails to interact with γ subunit variants with mutations or deletions in the C-terminal region.
source: This is in line with previous reports that the isolated γ subunit C-terminal tail interacts with the α subunit (Balsera et al., 2011; Dahinden et al., 2005), and the α subunit fails to interact with γ subunit variants with mutations or deletions in this region (Schmid et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Schmid et al., 2002.

claim: The ΔγCT truncation did not affect the protein level of the α subunit in the soluble fraction.
source: We found that the ΔγCT truncation did not affect the protein level of the α subunit in the soluble fraction (Figure 1—figure supplement 6a) or the interaction between the β and γ subunits (Figure 1—figure supplement 6b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the SDS-PAGE data in Figure 1—figure supplement 6a.

claim: The ΔγCT truncation did not affect the interaction between the β and γ subunits.
source: We found that the ΔγCT truncation did not affect the protein level of the α subunit in the soluble fraction (Figure 1—figure supplement 6a) or the interaction between the β and γ subunits (Figure 1—figure supplement 6b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the SDS-PAGE data in Figure 1—figure supplement 6b.

claim: The ΔγCT truncation severely reduced the amount of the α subunit co-purified with the βγ sub-complex.
source: However, it severely reduced the amount of the α subunit co-purified with the βγ sub-complex (Figure 1—figure supplement 6b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the SDS-PAGE data in Figure 1—figure supplement 6b.

claim: The γ subunit C-terminal tail is not involved in the interaction between the β and γ subunits but plays a critical role in the interaction between the α subunit and the βγ sub-complex.
source: These data indicate that the γ subunit C-terminal tail is not involved in the interaction between the β and γ subunits but plays a critical role in the interaction between the α subunit and the βγ sub-complex.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the ΔγCT truncation experiments.

claim: The β subunit is composed of 10 transmembrane helices (T1-10), two helical hairpins (H1a/b and H2a/b) and a number of additional helices.
source: The β subunit is composed of 10 transmembrane helices (T1-10), two helical hairpins (H1a/b and H2a/b) and a number of additional helices (Figure 1a and Figure 2a–c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in the structural figures.

claim: The N- and C-terminal halves of the β subunit form two repeats of inverted topology.
source: Its N- and C-terminal halves form two repeats of inverted topology (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in the topology diagram in Figure 2c.

claim: The region between T2 and T3' contains four helices (αE1-4), which form a solvent exposed domain E.
source: The region between T2 and T3' contains four helices (αE1-4), which form a solvent exposed domain E.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in the structural figures.

claim: Domain E is poorly conserved and does not exist in OAD in some organisms.
source: This domain is poorly conserved and does not exist in OAD in some organisms (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the sequence alignment in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: H1 and H2 point into the interior of the β subunit from opposite sides.
source: H1 and H2 point into the interior of the β subunit from opposite sides.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in the structural figures.

claim: H1 and H2 and surrounding helices T4-5 and T9-10 form a bundle-like core domain.
source: They and surrounding helices T4-5 and T9-10 form a bundle-like core domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in the structural figures.

claim: The tips of H1 and H2 meet at the middle of the core domain.
source: The tips of H1 and H2 meet at the middle of the core domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in the structural figures.

claim: The rest of the β subunit forms a scaffold domain, surrounding the core domain at one side.
source: The rest of the β subunit forms a scaffold domain, surrounding the core domain at one side (Figure 2a–b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2a-b.

claim: The closest structural homologue of the β subunit is the sodium/citrate symporter CitS.
source: A search through published structures (Holm and Rosenström, 2010) indicated that the closest structural homologue of the β subunit is the sodium/citrate symporter CitS (Kim et al., 2017; Wöhlert et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on a Dali server search.

claim: The structures of the Salmonella enterica CitS (SeCitS) and the β subunit can be superimposed with a root mean square deviation of 4.1 Å for equivalent Cα atoms.
source: The structures of the Salmonella enterica CitS (SeCitS) and the β subunit can be superimposed with a root mean square deviation of 4.1 Å for equivalent Cα atoms (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–b), despite their limited sequence identity (8%, Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The β subunit and SeCitS have limited sequence identity (8%).
source: The structures of the Salmonella enterica CitS (SeCitS) and the β subunit can be superimposed with a root mean square deviation of 4.1 Å for equivalent Cα atoms (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–b), despite their limited sequence identity (8%, Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in the sequence alignment in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: All major secondary structure elements in the β subunit core and scaffold domains have equivalents in CitS.
source: All major secondary structure elements in the β subunit core and scaffold domains have equivalents in CitS, which contains an extra helix at its N-terminus.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural comparison.

claim: CitS contains an extra helix at its N-terminus compared to the β subunit.
source: All major secondary structure elements in the β subunit core and scaffold domains have equivalents in CitS, which contains an extra helix at its N-terminus.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The β subunit belongs to the cation:proton antiporter (CPA) superfamily.
source: The β subunit belongs to the cation:proton antiporter (CPA) superfamily and has been suggested to have homology to proteins in the CPA2 family (http://www.tcdb.org/search/result.php?tc = 3.B.1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on database classification.

claim: The StOAD β subunit structure is homologous to the structure of the sodium/proton antiporter NapA.
source: Consistently, we found that the StOAD β subunit structure is homologous to the structure of the sodium/proton antiporter NapA (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a–b; Coincon et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2013), a member of the CPA2 family.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2, with citations to NapA structures.

claim: The β subunit has homology to sodium/proton antiporters NhaP and NhaA, the sodium/bile acid symporter ASBT and others.
source: It also has homology to sodium/proton antiporters NhaP (Paulino et al., 2014; Wöhlert et al., 2014) and NhaA (Hunte et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2014), the sodium/bile acid symporter ASBT (Hu et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2014) and others.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to structures of these proteins.

claim: The homology between the β subunit and its homologues is pronounced for the core domain.
source: The homology is pronounced for the core domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural comparison.

claim: Extensive interactions between the β subunits are observed in the structure.
source: Extensive interactions between the β subunits are observed in our structure.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the structural analysis.

claim: The interactions between β subunits are primarily mediated by the scaffold domain.
source: The interactions are primarily mediated by the scaffold domain (Figure 3a–b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3a-b.

claim: 2700 Å2 of surface area is buried at each interface between the scaffold domain in different β subunit monomers.
source: These interactions are primarily mediated by hydrophobic residue side chains. 2700 Å2 of surface area is buried at each interface between the scaffold domain in different monomers.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on calculation of buried surface area.

claim: 250 Å2 of surface area is buried at each interface between αE4 in different β subunit monomers.
source: Helix αE4 in domain E also makes a minor contribution to the trimer interface. 250 Å2 of surface area is buried at each interface between αE4 in different monomers.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on calculation of buried surface area.

claim: CitS forms a dimer.
source: Unlike the β subunit, the homologous CitS forms a dimer (Kim et al., 2017; Wöhlert et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to CitS structures.

claim: The large conformational differences between T1 and T6 and their equivalents in CitS play a key role in determining the oligomerization states.
source: Structural analysis indicated that the large conformational differences between T1 and T6 and their equivalents in CitS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b) plays a key role in determining the oligomerization states.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on structural comparison and inference.

claim: In the β subunit, T1 and T6 are located close to core domain.
source: In the β subunit, T1 and T6 are located close to core domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in the structural figures.

claim: In CitS, the equivalent H2 and H8 are located away from the core domain.
source: In CitS, the equivalent H2 and H8 are located away from the core domain (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: H2 and H1 N-terminal to it in CitS interact with H8 in the other monomer in the CitS dimer.
source: H2 and H1 N-terminal to it interact with H8 in the other monomer in the CitS dimer (Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The T1/T6 equivalents in CitS create a 'wedge' at the interface between monomers, which promotes dimer formation.
source: Compared to equivalent regions in the StOAD β subunit, these helices create a 'wedge' at the interface between monomers, which promotes dimer formation (Figure 3c–d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3c-d.

claim: Additional homologues of the β subunit including NapA and NhaP also form dimers.
source: Additional homologues of the β subunit including NapA (Coincon et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2013) and NhaP (Paulino et al., 2014; Wöhlert et al., 2014) also form dimers, similar structures are observed at their dimer interfaces (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b–c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b-c.

claim: The conformations of T1 and T6 are stabilized by extensive and mostly hydrophobic interactions with the neighboring T2 and T7, respectively.
source: The conformations of T1 and T6 are stabilized by extensive and mostly hydrophobic interactions with the neighboring T2 and T7, respectively (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Extensive interactions between the β and γ subunits are revealed by the structure.
source: Our structure also revealed extensive interactions between the β and γ subunits.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the structural analysis.

claim: Each γ subunit interacts with one β subunit.
source: Each γ subunit interacts with one β subunit (Figure 3—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1f.

claim: The interface between β and γ subunits buries 3100 Å2 of surface area and is primarily composed of residues with hydrophobic side chains.
source: The interface buries 3100 Å2 of surface area and is primarily composed of residues with hydrophobic side chains.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on calculation of buried surface area.

claim: T6 in the β subunit makes a significant contribution to the interface with the γ subunit.
source: T6 in the β subunit makes a significant contribution to the interface.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis.

claim: If T6 is located away from the core domain like its equivalent in CitS, it is not expected to interact with the γ subunit.
source: However, if it is located away from the core domain like its equivalent in CitS, it is not expected to interact with the γ subunit.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on inference from the structural comparison.

claim: The β/CitS protein no longer interacts with the γ subunit.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, we found that the substituted β/CitS protein no longer interacts with the γ subunit (Figure 3—figure supplement 1g), and is likely dimeric (Figure 3—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the co-purification experiments in Figure 3—figure supplement 1g.

claim: The β/CitS protein is likely dimeric.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, we found that the substituted β/CitS protein no longer interacts with the γ subunit (Figure 3—figure supplement 1g), and is likely dimeric (Figure 3—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the blue native PAGE data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1h.

claim: A large cavity opening to the periplasm is found at the center of the β subunit trimer.
source: A large cavity opening to the periplasm is found at the center of the β subunit trimer.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The densities in the large cavity at the center of the β subunit trimer were modeled as three n-dodecyl-D-maltoside (DDM) molecules.
source: The densities in it were modeled as three n-dodecyl-D-maltoside (DDM) molecules used in the complex purification (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The large cavity at the center of the β subunit trimer is primarily formed by residues with hydrophobic side chains in T3', T3 and T8.
source: This cavity is primarily formed by residues with hydrophobic side chains in T3', T3 and T8, suggesting that it may not contribute to sodium binding.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis.

claim: Each β subunit contains two negatively charged cavities in the cytoplasmic face.
source: In addition, each β subunit contains two negatively charged cavities in the cytoplasmic face.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The first cavity in the β subunit cytoplasmic face is formed between the core and scaffold domains, about 8 Å deep and measures 10 Å by 8 Å at the opening.
source: The first cavity is formed between the core and scaffold domains, about 8 Å deep and measures 10 Å by 8 Å at the opening.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis.

claim: The second cavity in the β subunit cytoplasmic face adjacent to the first is much shallower.
source: The second adjacent to it is much shallower (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The first cavity in the β subunit cytoplasmic face is highly conserved among decarboxylase sodium pumps.
source: The first cavity is highly conserved among decarboxylase sodium pumps, whereas residues in the second are more variable (Figure 1—figure supplement 5c–d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5c-d.

claim: Residues in the second cavity in the β subunit cytoplasmic face are more variable.
source: The first cavity is highly conserved among decarboxylase sodium pumps, whereas residues in the second are more variable (Figure 1—figure supplement 5c–d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5c-d.

claim: The first cavity in the β subunit cytoplasmic face may be a binding site for the positively charged sodium ion.
source: This suggests that the first cavity may be a binding site for the positively charged sodium ion, which should exist in all decarboxylase sodium pumps.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on inference from the conservation pattern and electrostatic properties.

claim: A sodium binding site is located between the tips of helical hairpins in CitS and at the equivalent positions in NhaP and ASBT.
source: A sodium binding site is located between the tips of helical hairpins in CitS and at the equivalent positions in NhaP and ASBT.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with implicit reference to published structures of these proteins.

claim: The H1 and H2 tips in the β subunit each contain one residue with polar or charged side chains, Asp203 and Ser382, respectively.
source: The H1 and H2 tips each contain one residue with polar or charged side chains, Asp203 and Ser382, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The side chains of Asp203 and Ser382 point into the space between the helical hairpin tips.
source: Their side chains point into the space between the helical hairpin tips (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The Asp203 and Ser382 side chains may participate in sodium binding.
source: Such structure suggests that the Asp203 and Ser382 side chains may participate in sodium binding.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on inference from the structural features.

claim: The ITC experiments revealed a Kd of 3.7 mM for sodium binding to the wild type StOAD βγ sub-complex.
source: The ITC experiments revealed a Kd of 3.7 mM for sodium binding to the wild type StOAD βγ sub-complex.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The D203A and S382A substitutions completely abolished sodium binding.
source: Remarkably, the D203A and S382A substitutions completely abolished sodium binding (Figure 4c, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—source data 1), indicating that the Asp203 and Ser382 side chains make critical contributions to sodium binding.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Asp203 and Ser382 side chains make critical contributions to sodium binding.
source: Remarkably, the D203A and S382A substitutions completely abolished sodium binding (Figure 4c, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—source data 1), indicating that the Asp203 and Ser382 side chains make critical contributions to sodium binding.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the ITC data showing loss of binding with these mutations.

claim: Continuous oxaloacetate decarboxylation by OAD requires sodium.
source: In line with the previous reports that continuous oxaloacetate decarboxylation by OAD requires sodium (Dimroth, 1982; Dimroth and Thomer, 1988) and a functional β subunit (Di Berardino and Dimroth, 1996; Jockel et al., 2000a; Jockel et al., 2000b), our activity assays indicated that these substitutions also severely inhibited oxaloacetate decarboxylation by StOAD.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to previous studies.

claim: Continuous oxaloacetate decarboxylation by OAD requires a functional β subunit.
source: In line with the previous reports that continuous oxaloacetate decarboxylation by OAD requires sodium (Dimroth, 1982; Dimroth and Thomer, 1988) and a functional β subunit (Di Berardino and Dimroth, 1996; Jockel et al., 2000a; Jockel et al., 2000b), our activity assays indicated that these substitutions also severely inhibited oxaloacetate decarboxylation by StOAD.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to previous studies.

claim: The D203A and S382A substitutions severely inhibited oxaloacetate decarboxylation by StOAD.
source: In line with the previous reports that continuous oxaloacetate decarboxylation by OAD requires sodium (Dimroth, 1982; Dimroth and Thomer, 1988) and a functional β subunit (Di Berardino and Dimroth, 1996; Jockel et al., 2000a; Jockel et al., 2000b), our activity assays indicated that these substitutions also severely inhibited oxaloacetate decarboxylation by StOAD.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Detergent-solubilized wild type StOAD βγ sub-complex strongly stimulated oxaloacetate decarboxylation by the α subunit in the presence of sodium.
source: Whereas detergent-solubilized wild type StOAD βγ sub-complex strongly stimulated oxaloacetate decarboxylation by the α subunit in the presence of sodium, such activity of the substituted StOAD βγ sub-complexes was lost (Figure 4d and Figure 4—source data 2).
